questions.question: In Xu’s URL shortener, the two primary REST-style endpoints are roughly:
options: POST to create a short URL; GET to resolve/redirect a short URL.
DELETE only, with no way to create or resolve aliases.
FTP upload of CSV files with no HTTP interface at all.
WebSocket-only binary frames with no resource URLs.
questions.explanation: URL shortening… POST… URL redirecting… GET

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
reference.excerpt: To create a new short URL, a client sends a POST request, which contains one parameter: the original long URL.

questions.question: A rate limiter in the HTTP world primarily:
options: Increases every client’s QPS without bound for fairness.
Limits how many client requests are allowed in a time window.
Replaces TLS certificates every millisecond automatically.
Stores all request bodies forever in browser localStorage.
questions.explanation: a rate limiter limits the number of client requests allowed to be sent over a specified period

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
reference.excerpt: In the HTTP world, a rate limiter limits the number of client requests allowed to be sent over a specified period.

questions.question: Xu lists a benefit of API rate limiting as:
options: Encouraging intentional DoS so capacity planning is realistic.
Preventing resource starvation from DoS (intentional or not) and reducing cost/load.
Removing the need for authentication on admin endpoints.
Guaranteeing unlimited free calls to paid third-party APIs.
questions.explanation: Prevent resource starvation caused by Denial of Service (DoS) attack… Reduce cost… Prevent servers from being overloaded

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
reference.excerpt: In this chapter, you are asked to design a rate limiter. Before starting the design, we first look at the benefits of using an API rate limiter: • Prevent resource starvation caused by Denial of Service (DoS) attack [1].

questions.question: Client-side-only rate limiting is weak because:
options: Browsers cannot send HTTP requests at all without it.
Clients can be forged/uncontrolled; enforcement belongs server-side or in middleware.
Servers are not allowed to count requests in distributed systems.
HTTP status codes cannot express throttling to clients.
questions.explanation: client is an unreliable place to enforce rate limiting because client requests can easily be forged

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
reference.excerpt: For now, we only need to know that the API gateway is a middleware that supports rate limiting.

questions.question: True or false: Xu’s rate limiter requirements include low latency, low memory, distributed use, clear exceptions, and fault tolerance.
questions.explanation: Low latency… little memory… Distributed rate limiting… Exception handling… High fault tolerance

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
reference.excerpt: Show clear exceptions to users when their requests are throttled. • High fault tolerance.

questions.question: When designing APIs in Step 2, you should:
options: Hide endpoints until after coding every storage engine quirk.
Propose endpoints and get interviewer buy-in before deep dives.
Only use SOAP envelopes with no resource naming.
Avoid status codes so clients guess success from latency.
questions.explanation: Propose high-level design and get buy-in

reference.book: System Design Interview – An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu
reference.excerpt: It is important to understand the requirements and clarify ambiguities Step 2 - Propose high-level design and get buy-in In this step, we aim to develop a high-level design and reach an agreement with the interviewer on the design.
